title: One Big Table vs Star Schema
summary: Cheap columnar storage made a once-heretical idea viable: pre-join everything into one wide table. It trades update efficiency for query simplicity, and knowing when that trade wins is a live modern debate.

slides.markdown:
For decades, [star schema](star-vs-snowflake-schema) was the unquestioned default for analytics. The modern challenger is **One Big Table (OBT)**: pre-join the fact and all its dimensions into a single wide table, so most reports need zero joins at all.

This isn't a rejection of dimensional modeling — it's a bet that cheap columnar storage and compute make the classic downsides of denormalization (storage duplication, update cost) small enough that query-time simplicity wins. Whether that bet pays off depends entirely on your specific update patterns and consumers, which is exactly what this topic works through.

**One Big Table** takes a fact table and its surrounding dimensions and joins them once, ahead of time, into a single flat table — every fact row now carries the customer's name, the product's category, the store's region, directly as columns, with no foreign keys left to resolve.

This is denormalization taken to its logical extreme: instead of star schema's "one join per dimension," OBT is "zero joins, ever," because the join already happened when the table was built. A BI tool or analyst querying it writes a plain `SELECT ... WHERE ... GROUP BY` against one table, full stop.

OBT isn't new as an idea — it's always been possible to pre-join tables. What changed is the cost of doing it at scale.

Columnar storage with dictionary encoding means a wide table with dozens of repeated dimension columns compresses close to the size of the fact table alone — the storage penalty that made OBT look wasteful in the 2000s is now a rounding error. And modern warehouse compute (serverless, auto-scaling, pay-per-query) makes the *rebuild* cost of a wide materialized table cheap and elastic, rather than requiring a fixed, provisioned ETL server running overnight batch jobs.

OBT is a consequence of infrastructure economics changing, not a new modeling insight.

| | OBT | Star schema |
|---|---|---|
| Joins at query time | None | One per dimension touched |
| Query authoring | Trivially simple, hard to get wrong | Requires knowing which dimension to join |
| Storage | Higher — every dimension attribute repeated per fact row | Lower — dimension data stored once |
| Update cost | A dimension attribute change requires rebuilding/updating the whole wide table | A dimension attribute change touches one row in one dimension table |
| Reuse across fact tables | Poor — a wide table is usually built for one specific fact | Strong — conformed dimensions serve many fact tables at once |

OBT wins on the query side; star wins on the update and reuse side. Neither number is small enough to ignore — the right choice depends on which side of the trade your actual workload pays more of.

The failure mode that catches teams off guard: an OBT built by joining five upstream sources means a schema or data change in *any one* of those five can force a full rebuild of the entire wide table, even if the other four sources didn't change at all.

Compare that to star schema, where the same upstream change touches exactly one dimension table — the others are untouched, and any fact table that already loaded is still valid. OBT's simplicity at query time is bought with **coupling** at build time: five independent upstream teams now share one blast radius, and a change any one of them makes can trigger a rebuild none of the others asked for.

This is a real operational cost that only shows up once the table has been in production a while and an upstream schema actually changes — which is exactly why it's easy to underestimate when first choosing OBT.

OBT earns its keep in a few specific situations:

- **BI-tool simplicity.** Many BI tools generate SQL from a drag-and-drop interface, and a single flat table with no join logic to configure is dramatically easier for a non-expert to use correctly.
- **ML feature tables.** A model training pipeline usually wants one row per training example with every feature already joined in — exactly OBT's shape — and doesn't care about update efficiency, because feature tables are often rebuilt wholesale on a schedule anyway.
- **Avoiding join mistakes by non-experts.** Every join is a chance to pick the wrong key or forget a filter; removing joins entirely removes that whole category of error for less experienced query authors.

In each case, the consumer's actual need — simplicity, or a training-ready shape — outweighs OBT's update-cost downside.

Star schema keeps its edge whenever:

- **Many fact tables share dimensions.** A [conformed](dimensional-modeling-basics) `dim_customer` referenced by ten fact tables means one update propagates everywhere; building ten separate OBTs would mean maintaining the same customer join logic ten times over, or the definitions drifting apart.
- **Update-heavy dimensions.** A dimension that changes frequently is expensive to keep current in a wide, rebuilt table but cheap to keep current as its own small table.
- **A general-purpose warehouse serving many unpredictable questions.** OBT is built for a specific consumer's shape; star schema's flexibility to join any combination of dimensions serves an open-ended set of future questions better.

The common thread: star schema wins when the workload is broad and shared, not narrow and specific.

OBT collapses "revenue by region and category" into a single-table scan:

```sql
-- OBT: everything pre-joined onto the fact row
SELECT region, category, SUM(revenue)
FROM obt_sales
GROUP BY region, category;
```

Against a star schema, the same question needs the fact joined to two dimensions:

```sql
-- star: two joins to reach region and category
SELECT s.region, p.category, SUM(f.revenue)
FROM fct_sales f
JOIN dim_store s   ON f.store_id   = s.store_id
JOIN dim_product p ON f.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY s.region, p.category;
```

Both return identical results. The OBT version is simpler to write and marginally faster at query time; the star version stays correct even if `dim_store` or `dim_product` gets new attributes tomorrow, with zero changes to the fact table.

Most mature warehouses don't pick one model exclusively — they run star schema as the durable, shared source of truth, and materialize OBT tables **on top of it** for specific consumers who need the flat shape.

The star schema stays the single place conformed dimensions are maintained and updated once. A nightly (or streaming) job then joins the relevant fact and dimensions into a wide table purpose-built for the BI tool or ML pipeline that wants it. If that OBT ever goes stale or wrong, it's disposable — rebuild it from the star schema, which remains the ground truth.

This gets both benefits: update efficiency and dimension reuse in the star layer, query simplicity in the OBT layer, at the cost of an extra materialization step most teams find worth paying.

A weak answer treats OBT vs star as a religious choice — "OBT is the modern way" or "star schema is the correct way." A strong answer identifies the actual consumer and their update-vs-query trade-off: is this table serving one BI dashboard or an ML pipeline (lean OBT), or is it the shared foundation many fact tables and teams build on (lean star, materialize OBT views on top as needed)?

The question an interviewer is really asking is whether you can reason about a schema decision from the workload backward, rather than reciting a rule.
